newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand markets reserve judgement on Peters.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand markets reserve judgement on Peters.

text.p: New Zealand financial markets have held back judging the appointment of Winston Peters to the powerful new role of Treasurer, analysts said on Monday.
They had taken comfort from details of a coalition agreement underwhich he was appointed, where the independence of the central bank has been confirmed and the price stability target relaxed.
Before the October election, markets were spooked by the rise of his New Zealand First Party because of stance against foreign investment, privatisation and desire to widen the target.
The demotion of Finance Minister Bill Birch to a junior role is a major concession by the senior coalition partner, National.
Parliamentary newcomer John Delamere, also of NZ First, becomes associate Treasurer and goes straight into the 20-strong cabinet unveiled on Sunday.

New Zealand First and National have outlined the detail of their coalition deal, which widens the current zero to two percent annual inflation target to zero to three percent and adds sustainable growth as a separate target.
The deal defers National's plan for a round of tax cuts in mid 1997 to 1998, to be replaced by additional spending -- NZ$5 billon over three years.
As Treasurer, Peters will write the budget but the exact nature of the division of labour between himself and Birch has yet to be released.
Bankers Trust NZ Chief Economist David Plank said National and NZ First had laid out a detailed blueprint in the agreement, the biggest change being alteration of the inflation target.
"Key to the deal was that the Reserve Bank has retained its independence and that the changes to the monetary regime, in my view, will not lead to any change in the way that monetary policy operates.
"Mr Peters may differ in that view, so it will be interesting to see how that develops over time," Plank said.
Peters' lack of experience in economics -- his background is in law -- was not a big issue, he said.

"The key is the quality of the advice that you get and I suppose being receptive to different sorts of advice and being able to evaluate that and against a blueprint or a framework that is consistent and holds together," he said.

"The coalition agreement means that there is a change in some economic policy but the fundamentals remain in place. If that is the way that policy continues to operate over the next few years then I don't think it's an improvement over what we've had, but I don't think it's a massive backward step.
"It's clearly a change in focus to much greater emphasis on spending and tolerance of slightly higher inflation," he said.
"People are reserving judgement (on Peters) at this stage, as they would on anybody," Plank said.
One analyst, who declined to be identified, said markets could take comfort from the detail of the agreement.
"In a sense that is consoling, but people are still fearful of the guy because in the past he has proven to be a bit volatile," he said.

Peters is a staunch proponent of a lower and more exporter-friendly New Zealand dollar and the currency has indeed fallen since the coalition deal, trading today at US$0.7005/12 from 0.7050 just before Tuesday's deal.

"The question is whether the currency will fall further and we think the chances of that happening are fairly limited," he said. "So one of the things that makes me nervous is that further down the track, like in three to six months time, with the currency still holding in there and possibly even higher, what do you do then?
Overseas markets appeared happy with what had happened, but there were still unknowns.
"We know where the power lies but just how it plays out will be interesting," the analyst said.

"But politically, he really has to make the whole thing work. His political future is at risk if he destabilises either the government or the financial markets. If he dies, it will all fall on his shoulders." -- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
